title: How a shared agreement about the kinds of people we are helping our children and students become affects learning
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton begins a new factor in his series by arguing that a school can only make learning its guiding idea if the whole community shares an agreement about what kinds of people it is helping children become. He recaps his working definition of learning and notes that learning can be good or bad, citing Fagin's pickpockets. Two stories carry the argument. England's cricket team turned around once a new leadership made clear what mattered, and then seemingly lost that clarity, and Skelton's own first headship stumbled when staff, governors and parents lacked a common view and a star teacher resigned. He concludes that undiscussed assumptions about what matters sit under every opinion of a school, and that explicit shared agreements shape the curriculum, behaviour, teaching and what students are asked to do.
points: A school can only be learning-focused if its community has explicitly agreed what kinds of people it wants to help children become.
Skelton's first headship shows how absent shared criteria send staff and parents into wary mutual judgement and divert energy from learning for roughly two years.
The England cricket example suggests clarity of purpose from leaders, believed by those they lead, can transform performance, but the clarity must be sustained.
Hidden assumptions about what matters underlie opinions about whether a school is good, so surfacing them is a precondition for sound decisions about curriculum and experiences.
quotes: Every view and opinion of what a school (or any organisation) does, whether it is ’good’ or ‘bad’, is often built on undiscussed and hidden views about what matters most.

In many organisations, a lack of shared agreement about what the organisation is for and what it is about wastes huge amounts of personal and organisational energy that can’t then be used where it should be used. Schools are just the same. The existence of shared agreements - or their absence - have profound implications about the kind, quality and quantity of learning that takes place.

For most of the year, we all danced warily around each other, judging each other without shared criteria. Through no one’s fault, other than a lack of a more sophisticated approach from all of us, this diverted our energy away from the children and their learning for far too long.

What helps enable schools and organisations to use learning as the frame of reference for all their decisions is the building of a shared agreement not only about whether learning should be central (it should) but also about what learning counts and how it is to happen. That shared agreement is also what is necessary to make sure that the student experience of learning in an organisation is both consistent and coherent.

They all bought in to it collectively and supported each other, always playing aggressively and never giving up the hope that the game was there for the winning. It was, and they did. But it was a shared agreement about what mattered that kicked off the change.

It’s down to us to make the choices about what learning matters for our children and students. It’s down to us to define the ‘good stuff’ we want children and students to learn. We can’t do that, though, unless we know what kinds of people we are hoping our children and students will become.
In other words, amidst all their complexities, successful organisations were driven everywhere by a core, single idea. In schools and similar organisations, that core idea has to be learning.
